sources.title: Buffers and the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: buffer action and the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. Verify against OpenStax Chemistry 2e, ch. 14 'Acid-Base Equilibria'.
sentences: A buffer is a solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.
It contains comparable amounts of a weak acid and its conjugate base, which neutralize added base and added acid respectively.
The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation states that pH equals pKa plus the logarithm of the ratio of conjugate base to weak acid.
When the concentrations of the weak acid and its conjugate base are equal, that logarithm is zero, so the pH equals the pKa.
Adding a small amount of strong acid to a buffer lowers the pH only slightly, because the conjugate base neutralizes and consumes most of the added hydrogen ions.
To hold the pH one unit above the pKa, the ratio of conjugate base to weak acid must be about ten to one.

sources.title: Gibbs free energy and spontaneity
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: Gibbs free energy criterion for spontaneity. Verify against OpenStax Chemistry 2e, ch. 16 'Thermodynamics'.
sentences: The Gibbs free energy change determines whether a reaction is spontaneous at constant temperature and pressure.
It is defined as the enthalpy change minus the temperature times the entropy change.
A reaction is spontaneous when its Gibbs free energy change is negative.
When both the enthalpy change and the entropy change are positive, raising the temperature can make the reaction spontaneous once the temperature times entropy term exceeds the enthalpy change.
A positive enthalpy change alone does not forbid spontaneity, because a large favorable entropy change can still drive the reaction.

sources.title: Catalysts and activation energy
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: catalysis and activation energy. Verify against OpenStax Chemistry 2e, ch. 12 'Kinetics'.
sentences: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by providing an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy.
It lowers the activation energy for the forward and reverse directions equally.
Because it does not change the free energy difference between reactants and products, a catalyst does not shift the position of the equilibrium.
A catalyst is not consumed by the reaction and does not change the reaction enthalpy.

sources.title: Competitive versus noncompetitive enzyme inhibition
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: reversible enzyme inhibition and its effect on kinetic parameters. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 6 'Metabolism'.
sentences: A competitive inhibitor binds the enzyme's active site and competes directly with the substrate.
Competitive inhibition raises the apparent Michaelis constant while leaving the maximum velocity unchanged.
Its effect can be overcome by adding a large excess of substrate, which outcompetes the inhibitor.
A noncompetitive inhibitor binds an allosteric site away from the active site, whether or not substrate is bound.
Noncompetitive inhibition lowers the maximum velocity while leaving the Michaelis constant unchanged.
Because it does not compete for the active site, adding more substrate cannot reverse noncompetitive inhibition.

sources.title: Michaelis-Menten kinetics: maximum velocity and the Michaelis constant
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 6 'Metabolism'.
sentences: Enzyme-catalyzed reactions often follow Michaelis-Menten kinetics, giving a hyperbolic curve of initial rate versus substrate concentration.
The maximum velocity is the rate approached when the enzyme is saturated with substrate.
The maximum velocity equals the catalytic rate constant times the total enzyme concentration, so using less enzyme lowers the maximum velocity.
The Michaelis constant is the substrate concentration at which the reaction runs at half its maximum velocity, and it reflects substrate affinity rather than the amount of enzyme.

sources.title: Degeneracy of the genetic code and mutation types
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: redundancy of the genetic code and point/frameshift mutations. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 15 'Genes and Proteins'.
sentences: The genetic code is degenerate, meaning most amino acids are specified by more than one codon.
A single-base change that still codes for the same amino acid is a silent mutation and leaves the protein sequence unchanged.
A frameshift mutation, caused by an insertion or deletion, shifts the reading frame and usually changes many downstream amino acids.
A nonsense mutation converts a codon into a stop codon and truncates the protein.

sources.title: Glycolysis, fermentation, and the electron transport chain
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: cellular respiration and anaerobic fermentation. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 7 'Cellular Respiration'.
sentences: Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate and yields a small net gain of ATP without requiring oxygen.
It also reduces the carrier NAD+ to NADH, which must be reoxidized for glycolysis to continue.
Under aerobic conditions the electron transport chain regenerates NAD+ and produces most of the cell's ATP.
Under anaerobic conditions the electron transport chain stalls, so muscle cells ferment pyruvate into lactate to regenerate NAD+ and keep glycolysis running.

sources.title: The spacing effect (distributed practice)
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: the spacing effect. Verify against Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted & Rohrer (2006), Psychological Bulletin 132(3), 354-380.
sentences: The spacing effect is the finding that study distributed over several sessions is retained better than the same amount of study massed into one session.
Distributed practice produces stronger long-term retention than cramming even when the total study time is held constant.
To show that the benefit comes from spacing rather than the mere passage of time, an experiment should compare massed and spaced groups matched on total study time.
The spacing benefit is largest on a delayed test and can be hidden when retention is measured immediately after study.

sources.title: The testing effect (retrieval practice)
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: the testing effect. Verify against Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Psychological Science 17(3), 249-255.
sentences: The testing effect, also called retrieval practice, is the finding that actively recalling information strengthens memory more than simply rereading it.
Retrieval practice can improve later retention even when it takes less total time than repeated study.
Adding corrective feedback after each retrieval attempt further improves learning by letting students fix their errors.

sources.title: The serial position effect: primacy and recency
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: serial position, primacy, and recency effects. Verify against Murdock (1962), Journal of Experimental Psychology 64(5), 482-488.
sentences: The serial position effect describes better recall for items at the beginning and the end of a list than for items in the middle.
The primacy effect is the superior recall of the first items, attributed to their extra rehearsal into long-term memory.
The recency effect is the superior recall of the last items, attributed to their lingering in short-term memory.

sources.title: Attribution biases: self-serving bias and the fundamental attribution error
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: attribution biases. Verify against Ross (1977), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology 10, 173-220.
sentences: The self-serving bias is the tendency to attribute one's own successes to internal factors like ability and one's failures to external factors like circumstances.
The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to overweight personality and underweight the situation when explaining other people's behavior.
The actor-observer bias is the related tendency to explain one's own behavior by the situation but others' behavior by their disposition.

sources.title: On translation and loss (CARS-style humanities passage)
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Original authored prose written for CARS reasoning practice; the argument (translation entails choosing which loss to accept) is the author's own and not attributed to another work.
sentences: Every translation is an argument about what a text is for.
A translator who keeps a poem's literal sense treats meaning as cargo to be carried across intact, while one who reworks its rhythm treats the poem as an experience to be reproduced.
Neither approach is simply right, since the first risks an accurate but lifeless rendering and the second risks writing a new poem under another author's name.
Languages do not encode one fixed set of ideas but carve the world at different joints, so a translation with no loss at all is impossible.
To ask for a translation that loses nothing is to ask for the original, which is the one thing the reader cannot read.

sources.title: Strong versus weak acids (distractor)
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: acid strength and dissociation. Verify against OpenStax Chemistry 2e, ch. 14 'Acid-Base Equilibria'.
sentences: A strong acid dissociates completely in water, while a weak acid only partially dissociates.
The lower the pKa, the stronger the acid and the more completely it donates protons.
Adding a strong acid to pure water lowers the pH sharply because there is nothing to neutralize the added hydrogen ions.

sources.title: Osmosis and tonicity (distractor)
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: osmosis and tonicity. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 5 'Structure and Function of Plasma Membranes'.
sentences: Osmosis is the passive movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from lower to higher solute concentration.
A cell placed in a hypertonic solution loses water and shrinks, while one in a hypotonic solution gains water and may burst.
Osmosis does not consume ATP, because it is driven by the water concentration gradient rather than by an active pump.

sources.title: Operant conditioning and reinforcement schedules (distractor)
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: operant conditioning and reinforcement schedules. Verify against Skinner (1938), 'The Behavior of Organisms'.
sentences: In operant conditioning, behavior is shaped by its consequences: reinforcement increases a behavior and punishment decreases it.
A variable-ratio schedule, which rewards behavior after an unpredictable number of responses, produces high and steady response rates.
Negative reinforcement increases a behavior by removing an unpleasant stimulus, and is not the same as punishment.

sources.title: Controlled experiments: controls, confounds, and random assignment
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: controlled experiments, controls, confounds, isolating variables, and random assignment. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 1 'The Study of Life' and OpenStax Psychology 2e, ch. 2 'Psychological Research'.
sentences: A controlled experiment compares a treatment group with a control group that is treated identically except for the one variable being tested.
A confounding variable is a second factor that changes along with the treatment, so a difference in the outcome cannot be attributed to the treatment alone.
To isolate the effect of one variable, the experimenter holds all other conditions constant and changes only that variable between the groups.
Conditions such as temperature must be kept the same across the groups, because temperature is itself a variable that changes many reaction and enzyme rates.
If two variables are changed at the same time, their effects are confounded and the difference in the result cannot be assigned to either variable by itself.
Randomly assigning participants to the groups controls for confounding differences between people, such as motivation, that self-selection would otherwise introduce.
A solvent control receives the same solvent but not the active substance, so any effect can be traced to the substance rather than to the solvent it was dissolved in.

sources.title: Cellular Metabolism: Enzymes, Glycolysis, and Oxidative Phosphorylation (chapter)
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: cellular metabolism (enzyme catalysis, glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation). Original author-written chapter, released CC0-1.0; nothing is copied verbatim. Verify each fact against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 6 'Metabolism' and ch. 7 'Cellular Respiration and Fermentation'. This is the single chapter source from which the card-check generator produces its 50 candidate cards.
sentences: Metabolism is the sum of an organism's chemical reactions, split into catabolism that releases energy by breaking molecules down and anabolism that spends energy to build molecules up.
An enzyme is a biological catalyst that lowers a reaction's activation energy without being consumed or shifting the reaction's equilibrium.
The pocket of an enzyme that binds substrate and carries out the chemistry is called the active site.
In the induced-fit model, binding of the substrate reshapes the active site so that it grips the substrate more snugly.
Every enzyme has an optimal temperature and pH at which its catalytic rate peaks, and drifting away from that optimum slows the enzyme down.
Most enzymes in the human body work fastest near 37 degrees Celsius, and excessive heat denatures them by unfolding their three-dimensional shape.
A cofactor is a nonprotein partner an enzyme requires to function, and when that partner is a small organic molecule derived from a vitamin it is termed a coenzyme.
In feedback inhibition, the final product of a metabolic pathway binds and switches off an enzyme that acts early in the same pathway.
An allosteric regulator binds an enzyme at a site separate from the active site and thereby raises or lowers the enzyme's activity.
Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and cleaves a single six-carbon glucose into a pair of three-carbon pyruvate molecules.
The net payoff of glycolysis is two ATP and two NADH per glucose, and the pathway proceeds even in the complete absence of oxygen.
Glycolysis opens with an energy investment phase that spends two ATP to phosphorylate glucose before any ATP is harvested.
Under aerobic conditions, each pyruvate is oxidized and joined to coenzyme A to form acetyl-CoA while releasing carbon dioxide.
The citric acid cycle, also known as the Krebs cycle, runs in the mitochondrial matrix and finishes oxidizing glucose-derived carbon to carbon dioxide.
Each turn of the citric acid cycle generates three NADH, one FADH2, and one GTP.
The electron transport chain is embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane and relays electrons from NADH and FADH2 toward a final acceptor.
Oxygen serves as the final electron acceptor of the electron transport chain and is reduced to water at the end of the chain.
As electrons pass down the chain, protons are driven from the matrix into the intermembrane space, storing energy as an electrochemical proton gradient.
ATP synthase taps the proton gradient by letting protons flow back into the matrix, and it couples that flow to attaching phosphate to ADP in a process called chemiosmosis.
Fully oxidizing one glucose by aerobic respiration yields roughly 30 to 32 ATP in a typical human cell.
Oxidative phosphorylation supplies the large majority of a cell's ATP, far outstripping the modest yield from glycolysis alone.
When oxygen runs out, the electron transport chain halts and leaves the NADH from earlier steps stuck in its reduced form.
In the absence of oxygen, human muscle cells run lactic acid fermentation, converting pyruvate into lactate to regenerate NAD+.
Fermentation restores the NAD+ that glycolysis depends on, yet it delivers no ATP beyond the small amount glycolysis already produced.
Gluconeogenesis assembles new glucose from noncarbohydrate sources such as certain amino acids, and it is not simply glycolysis running in reverse.
Insulin, released when blood sugar is high, lowers blood glucose by prompting cells to take up glucose and store it as glycogen.
Glucagon, released when blood sugar is low, raises blood glucose largely by triggering the breakdown of glycogen in the liver.
Beta-oxidation chops fatty acids into two-carbon acetyl-CoA units that feed the citric acid cycle and ultimately yield a large amount of ATP.
An enzyme's reaction rate rises with substrate concentration until the active sites are saturated, at which point the rate levels off at its maximum velocity.
The Michaelis constant is the substrate concentration at which an enzyme works at half of its maximum velocity, and a smaller value indicates tighter substrate binding.

sources.title: The central dogma: transcription and translation
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: the central dogma, transcription, and translation. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 15 'Genes and Proteins'.
sentences: The central dogma of molecular biology describes the flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA to protein.
During transcription, RNA polymerase reads a DNA template strand and builds a complementary messenger RNA molecule.
In eukaryotes the new transcript gains a cap and a poly-A tail and has its introns spliced out before the messenger RNA leaves the nucleus.
During translation, the ribosome reads the messenger RNA in three-base codons and joins the matching amino acids into a polypeptide.
Transfer RNA molecules carry specific amino acids and pair their anticodons with the codons on the messenger RNA.

sources.title: DNA replication
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: DNA replication. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 14 'DNA Structure and Function'.
sentences: DNA replication is semiconservative, so each daughter molecule keeps one parental strand and pairs it with one newly made strand.
Helicase unwinds the double helix at the replication fork and separates the two template strands.
DNA polymerase can only extend a strand, so it needs a short primer before it can begin adding new nucleotides.
The leading strand is copied continuously, while the lagging strand is made in short Okazaki fragments that DNA ligase later joins together.

sources.title: Prokaryotic cell structure, growth, and genetics
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: structure, growth, and genetics of prokaryotic cells. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 22 'Prokaryotes: Bacteria and Archaea'.
sentences: In a prokaryotic cell the single circular chromosome sits in a region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid, since a prokaryote lacks a membrane-bound nucleus.
Most bacteria are wrapped in a peptidoglycan cell wall, and the Gram stain sorts them by how much peptidoglycan that wall holds.
Bacteria reproduce asexually by binary fission, copying the chromosome and splitting into two identical daughter cells.
Bacteria gain new genes horizontally through transformation, transduction, and conjugation, which can spread traits such as antibiotic resistance.

sources.title: Virus structure and replication cycles
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: virus structure and viral life cycles. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 21 'Viruses'.
sentences: A virus genome of DNA or RNA is enclosed in a protein coat called a capsid.
Because a virus cannot reproduce on its own, it must hijack a living host cell and use that cell's machinery to copy itself.
In the lytic cycle the bacteriophage bursts the host cell and makes new virus particles, while in the lysogenic cycle its DNA integrates into the host genome and stays dormant.
A retrovirus such as HIV carries an RNA genome and uses reverse transcriptase to copy that RNA into DNA inside the host cell.

sources.title: The cell cycle and mitosis
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: the cell cycle and mitosis. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 10 'Cell Reproduction'.
sentences: The cell cycle alternates between interphase, when the cell grows and copies its DNA, and mitosis, when the duplicated chromosomes are divided.
During mitosis the spindle apparatus attaches to the chromosomes and pulls the identical sister chromatids toward opposite poles of the cell.
Checkpoints run by cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases hold the cell cycle until each stage is finished correctly.

sources.title: Cell differentiation, stem cells, and early development
sources.author: Vantage (synthetic, author-written)
sources.citation: Concept: cell differentiation, stem cells, gametogenesis, and embryogenesis. Verify against OpenStax Biology 2e, ch. 43 'Animal Reproduction and Development'.
sentences: During differentiation an unspecialized cell turns on a specific set of genes and becomes a specialized cell type.
A stem cell is unspecialized and can both renew itself and give rise to more specialized cells.
After fertilization the zygote undergoes cleavage into a ball of cells and then gastrulation, which forms the three germ layers of the embryo.
Gametogenesis produces gametes through meiosis, forming sperm in males and egg cells in females.
